title: Zero Downtime Upgrade Workflow Automation: 5 Tools
summary: Zero downtime upgrade workflow automation requires separating concerns: use orchestrators like Temporal for the upgrade process, workflows for approvals.
body_markdown:
## Argo Rollouts traffic shifting on Kubernetes


If you run on Kubernetes, Argo Rollouts is the traffic-owning tool that pairing calls for. It replaces the Deployment object with one that shifts traffic in stages and reverses itself when metrics turn bad.


### Blue-green and canary upgrade strategies


Most teams are still on rolling updates by default.


In the[Vamp survey reported by InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2021/03/vamp-state-cloud-native-release/) , 57% of participants used them in production, against 22% for blue-green, 9% for canary and 7% for big-bang, so this approach has effectively become the standard in real-world deployment scenarios.


So most teams replace pods gradually and have no controlled way to hold back a bad version. Only about three in ten use blue-green or canary, the two strategies Argo Rollouts adds, and that gap's the case for adopting it.


### Automated analysis and rollback


During a canary, Rollouts can pause at set weights and run an analysis against your metrics provider. If error rate or latency crosses the threshold you defined, it aborts and returns traffic to the stable version without anyone paging a human.


Written down as a query you can review in advance, the rollback decision is therefore not made under pressure at 2 a.m.


Because Rollouts works only on Kubernetes workloads, databases, virtual machines and anything outside the cluster need another mechanism.


It also has little to offer for human coordination: a rollout can pause for manual promotion, but there's no approval chain, no record of who signed off and no notification routing.


For the visibility that layer needs, look at a queue dashboard such as Bull-Board. Its overview here lists 132 active and 136 failed jobs across billing, email, notification and report queues, which means failures roughly match work in flight and someone has to see them.


For approvals, Argo gives you nothing equivalent, which is the job of the lighter workflow tool in the next part of the setup.


**Activepieces fills that approval gap** without pretending to be a deploy engine, and its catalogue is something you can count yourself: the 750 integrations are the entries in the` packages/pieces/community` directory of the[open-source monorepo on GitHub](https://github.com/activepieces/activepieces/tree/main/packages/pieces/community) , counted from that directory rather than quoted from a marketing page, so you're assessing what's genuinely available rather than what a sales claim suggests.


The core is under the MIT licence, and roughly 60% of those integrations were contributed by the community.


If your ingress or deploy tool has no integration, you can generate one with AI and keep it private to your own instance, so the approval step never waits on a vendor release. MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run it in production.
